connection: Session 18 studied interface polymorphism. Nothing in the real practice-07092026 source uses inheritance or abstract classes at all -- this session introduces HoursPolicyBase, a new, clearly-labeled abstract class that StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy now inherit from, and previews PayrollDbContext's real inheritance from EF Core's DbContext (Session 31).
objectives: Explain what HoursPolicyBase adds beyond what IHoursPolicy alone already provided: a shared, non-abstract Round helper both derived classes inherit for free.
Distinguish HoursPolicyBase's abstract GetVariance (each derived class must supply its own) from its concrete Round (shared, inherited, never overridden).
Confirm StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance's override keyword is required, and explain what the compiler checks it against.
Preview why PayrollDbContext (Session 31) will be this codebase's first real, necessary use of inheritance -- EF Core requires a DbContext subclass, not just an interface implementation.

visuals.title: An abstract class can mix required and shared members
visuals.explanation: HoursPolicyBase declares GetVariance as abstract (each subclass must implement it) and Round as a concrete, shared protected method (subclasses inherit it unchanged).

visuals.title: override is checked against the abstract declaration
visuals.explanation: StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance must use override, and its signature must match HoursPolicyBase's abstract declaration exactly, or the compiler rejects it.

visuals.title: Round is never duplicated
visuals.explanation: Neither StandardHoursPolicy nor FlexibleHoursPolicy defines its own Round method -- both inherit the single implementation from HoursPolicyBase.

visuals.title: An interface alone could not have done this
visuals.explanation: IHoursPolicy could declare GetVariance, but interfaces (before default interface members) cannot supply Round's shared implementation the way an abstract base class can.

preQuiz.prompt: What could HoursPolicyBase do that IHoursPolicy alone could not?
options: Provide Round as a real, shared method body that both StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy inherit without rewriting it -- an interface can declare a member's signature but an ordinary interface cannot supply reusable implementation the way an abstract class can
Nothing -- interfaces and abstract classes are functionally identical
Prevent FlexibleHoursPolicy from ever changing its GetVariance result
preQuiz.explanation: This is the concrete difference this session demonstrates: shared, inherited implementation is an abstract class capability that a plain interface does not give you.

preQuiz.prompt: Why must StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance use the override keyword?
options: HoursPolicyBase declares GetVariance as abstract, which requires every concrete derived class to supply an implementation marked override -- the compiler checks the signature matches exactly
override is required by IHoursPolicy, not HoursPolicyBase
preQuiz.explanation: abstract members create a contract just as binding as an interface member -- override is how C# confirms a derived class is fulfilling that specific abstract declaration, not just adding an unrelated method with the same name.

preQuiz.prompt: Why will PayrollDbContext (Session 31) be forced to use inheritance, when nothing else in this codebase has needed it?
options: EF Core's design requires your context class to literally BE a DbContext (public class PayrollDbContext : DbContext), inheriting its real infrastructure (change tracking, SaveChangesAsync) -- there is no interface-based alternative for that specific framework requirement
It isn't forced to -- it's a stylistic choice
DbContext is an interface, not a base class
preQuiz.explanation: This is a genuine, external constraint from the EF Core framework itself, not a design preference this course is choosing -- worth previewing now so Session 31's inheritance doesn't feel unmotivated.

concept.title: HoursPolicyBase: abstract plus concrete, in one class
paragraphs: public abstract class HoursPolicyBase : IHoursPolicy declares GetVariance as abstract decimal GetVariance(decimal recordedHours) -- no body, forcing every non-abstract derived class to supply one.
The same class also declares protected static decimal Round(decimal hours) with a real, complete body -- every derived class inherits this exact implementation; none of them re-declare it.

concept.title: Two derived classes, one required override, one free inheritance
paragraphs: StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy both extend HoursPolicyBase now, instead of implementing IHoursPolicy directly. Each provides its own override decimal GetVariance(...) -- required, because GetVariance is abstract.
Neither class writes its own Round method -- both simply call the inherited one, exactly as HoursPolicyBase defined it, with zero duplication.

concept.title: A preview: PayrollDbContext's real, necessary inheritance
paragraphs: Session 31 introduces PayrollDbContext : DbContext -- EF Core's own design requires your context type to literally be a DbContext, gaining its real change-tracking and SaveChangesAsync machinery through inheritance.

This is different from HoursPolicyBase's inheritance, which this course chose deliberately to demonstrate the concept -- PayrollDbContext's inheritance is externally required by the EF Core framework itself, the first genuinely necessary use of inheritance in this codebase.

lab.objective: Confirm HoursPolicyBase's split between abstract and concrete members, and that both derived policies inherit Round unchanged.
lab.startingCondition: HoursPolicyBase, StandardHoursPolicy, and FlexibleHoursPolicy already exist with the real abstract/concrete split.
steps: Attempt to instantiate HoursPolicyBase directly (new HoursPolicyBase()) and confirm the compiler rejects it -- abstract classes cannot be constructed.
Remove the override keyword from StandardHoursPolicy.GetVariance and confirm the compiler rejects the resulting method as an unrelated overload, not a valid override.
Confirm neither StandardHoursPolicy nor FlexibleHoursPolicy declares its own Round method, and that GetVariance's rounded results still work correctly through the inherited one.
Run the existing HoursPolicyTests.cs and confirm both policies still pass with their real, unchanged expected values.
lab.expectedBehavior: HoursPolicyBase cannot be constructed directly; removing override causes a compile error; both policies correctly use the inherited Round method with no duplication; existing tests pass unchanged.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Confirm HoursPolicyBase's real abstract/concrete member split and both derived classes.
Confirm existing coverage still passes against the now-inherited implementation.
Publish synchronized lesson, lab, and quiz material.

commit: session-18: teach abstract classes inheritance and overrides
review: HoursPolicyBase is explicitly introduced as new, since no real inheritance exists in the source app.
The abstract/concrete split (GetVariance vs Round) is demonstrated by actually attempting to instantiate the base class and remove the override keyword.
PayrollDbContext's future, genuinely-required inheritance is previewed honestly as a different motivation than this session's deliberate teaching example.
The full test suite passes with both policies working correctly through the new inheritance chain.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can't HoursPolicyBase be instantiated directly with new HoursPolicyBase()?
options: It is declared abstract, and abstract classes can never be constructed directly -- only concrete (non-abstract) derived classes like StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy can be instantiated
postQuiz.explanation: abstract on a class is exactly this: a promise that the class is incomplete on its own and exists only to be extended.

postQuiz.prompt: If HoursPolicyBase's Round method were declared virtual instead of a plain (non-virtual) method, what new capability would that add?
options: Derived classes could optionally override Round with their own rounding behavior, using the override keyword -- today, neither StandardHoursPolicy nor FlexibleHoursPolicy can customize it at all
postQuiz.explanation: virtual is what opens a concrete method up to being overridden; a plain method (like Round today) is fixed for every derived class, which is exactly why neither policy can (or needs to) customize rounding.

postQuiz.prompt: What is genuinely different about PayrollDbContext's future inheritance from DbContext, compared to StandardHoursPolicy's inheritance from HoursPolicyBase?
options: PayrollDbContext's inheritance is required by the EF Core framework's own design; HoursPolicyBase's inheritance was a deliberate choice this course made specifically to have a real example to teach from
There is no real difference between the two
PayrollDbContext will not actually use inheritance
postQuiz.explanation: This distinction matters for judgment: not every inheritance relationship is equally motivated -- some are genuinely required by a framework, others are a design choice worth justifying on their own merits.

reflections: Why did this course choose to add a new abstract class (HoursPolicyBase) rather than leave Session 19 without any real inheritance example at all?
What would you lose if HoursPolicyBase's Round method were duplicated separately inside StandardHoursPolicy and FlexibleHoursPolicy instead of shared?
Now that you've seen both an interface-only design (Session 18's original IHoursPolicy) and an abstract-class design (this session's HoursPolicyBase), when would you reach for each?
whatBreaks: Attempting new HoursPolicyBase() directly fails to compile, because abstract classes exist only to be extended, never instantiated on their own. Removing StandardHoursPolicy's override keyword from GetVariance produces a compile error, because the compiler can no longer connect that method to HoursPolicyBase's abstract declaration. Duplicating Round's logic separately inside each derived policy (instead of inheriting it) would reintroduce the exact kind of duplication generics (Session 14) and interfaces (Session 18) already exist to avoid.
summary: HoursPolicyBase is a new, clearly-labeled abstract class -- nothing in the real source uses inheritance, so this session builds one specifically to demonstrate what an abstract class adds beyond an interface: a required abstract member (GetVariance) alongside a shared, concrete, inherited one (Round). Session 31's PayrollDbContext will be this codebase's first genuinely framework-required use of inheritance, previewed here so it does not feel unmotivated when it arrives.
